figures.title: Kalshi Scored Better in 11 of 14 Competitive Senate Races
figures.subtitle: Each bar compares errors in one resolved race. Left favors Kalshi; right favors the mixed forecast.

figures.title: Kalshi’s Advantage Remains When Any One Race Is Excluded
figures.subtitle: Removing Kansas reduces the advantage more than removing any other race, but the remaining comparison still favors Kalshi.

figures.title: Changing the Race Sample Does Not Reverse Kalshi’s Advantage
figures.subtitle: These ranges reflect the observed mix of races, not performance across different national election environments.

figures.title: Correlated Races Widen the Range of Plausible Scores
figures.subtitle: The lines show how widely losses can vary under each source’s probabilities and two assumptions about races moving together.

figures.title: More Kalshi Weight Coincided with Lower Loss
figures.subtitle: Neither the Economist–VoteHub average nor its equal blend with Kalshi achieved a lower loss than Kalshi alone.

figures.title: Longshots Recorded 2 Wins Against 3.13 Expected
figures.subtitle: Observed and probability-based expected wins are compared within the same eligible races.

figures.title: Softening Lean and Likely Probabilities Improved Cook’s Score
figures.subtitle: The softer Wide mapping had the lowest loss across the three approved Cook conversions.

figures.title: Correlated Races Make Small Accuracy Gaps Harder to Detect
figures.subtitle: Shared movement leaves less independent evidence for detecting small accuracy gaps.
